query_text: What medicine should I take when I get a cold?

content.text:
For a typical **common cold**, medicines don’t “cure” it—they mainly **reduce symptoms** while your body recovers. Most colds improve on their own in about **7–10 days**. Antibiotics don’t help a cold because colds are usually viral. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

**Common options for adults:**

- **Fever, sore throat, headache, body aches:**  
  **Acetaminophen** or **ibuprofen** can help. Follow the label dosing. Avoid doubling up—many “multi-symptom” cold products already contain acetaminophen. ([mayoclinic.org](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/common-cold/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20351611?sf237848573=1&utm_source=openai))

- **Stuffy nose / congestion:**  
  A **saline nasal spray**, steam/humidifier, or an OTC **decongestant** may help. Avoid oral decongestants like pseudoephedrine/phenylephrine if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure, certain heart conditions, glaucoma, prostate/urination problems, or are on some antidepressants—ask a pharmacist/clinician.

- **Runny nose / sneezing:**  
  An **antihistamine** may help, but some cause drowsiness and dry mouth.

- **Cough:**  
  **Honey** can soothe cough for adults and children over 1 year old. OTC cough medicines may help some people, but effects are often modest. Do **not** give honey to infants under 1 year.

- **General care:**  
  Rest, fluids, warm tea/soup, saltwater gargles, and a humidifier can help symptoms.

**Important for children:** OTC cough/cold medicines are **not recommended for children younger than 6** by the CDC, and the FDA warns against cough/cold products in children under 2 due to potentially serious side effects. Ask a pediatrician or pharmacist before giving cold medicine to a child. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

**Get medical advice urgently** if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, blue lips, confusion, severe dehydration, fever that’s high or lasts more than a few days, symptoms that improve then worsen, or if you’re high-risk—pregnant, older adult, immunocompromised, or have chronic heart/lung disease. Also consider COVID/flu testing if symptoms fit or you’ve been exposed.
